question: Early in aviation history, most accidents were caused by equipment failure. Over the last several decades the dominant cause has shifted mainly because:

options.text: Airframes, engines and avionics became far more reliable, leaving human performance as the factor that did not improve at the same rate
Weather forecasting became less accurate
Pilots began flying more hours per year than in earlier decades
Regulators stopped investigating mechanical causes

explanation: Reliability engineering greatly reduced mechanical and navigational failures, but the human being was not redesigned to match. The result is that human performance now accounts for the clear majority of accident causes, not because people got worse, but because the other causes got better.

question: Investigators now generally prefer the term "human error" to the older term "pilot error" because:

options.text: The two terms mean exactly the same thing and the change is only stylistic
"Pilot error" implies the flight crew was the only link in the chain, while most occurrences involve contributions from design, procedures, training or maintenance as well
"Human error" is shorter to write in a report
"Pilot error" is a legal term that cannot be used outside a courtroom

explanation: A single crew action is rarely the whole story. "Human error" deliberately widens the frame to include designers, maintainers, controllers and managers, all of whom can plant the conditions for an error long before a pilot ever touches the controls.

question: Human Factors, as applied to aviation, is best described as:

options.text: The study of people, their relationship with equipment, procedures and the working environment, and with each other, aimed at safety and efficiency
A set of fitness tests taken before each medical renewal
A legal framework that assigns blame after an accident
A branch of aerodynamics concerned with cockpit airflow

explanation: Human Factors is a systems discipline: it looks at the person, the machine, the procedures and the people around them together, with the twin goals of safety and operational efficiency, rather than at any one of those in isolation.

question: In James Reason's "Swiss Cheese" model of accident causation, each layer of organizational defence (design, procedures, supervision, training and so on) is drawn as a slice with holes because:

options.text: Every defence has weaknesses, and those weaknesses open and close over time rather than staying fixed
Only one layer of defence actually matters in practice
The holes represent deliberate sabotage rather than ordinary weaknesses
The model applies only to maintenance, not to flight operations

explanation: No single defence is perfect. The holes are the gaps that latent conditions and active failures create, and they move and change size as circumstances change. An accident needs the holes in several slices to line up at the same moment.

question: For an accident to occur under Reason's model, which of the following must happen?

options.text: A single defence must fail completely while all others remain perfect
The holes in every layer of defence must align at the same moment, letting a trajectory of failure pass straight through
The aircraft must already be outside its normal flight envelope
An active failure must occur without any latent condition being present

explanation: The model's central image is alignment: an accident trajectory passes through the system only when gaps in several independent defences happen to coincide. Any one layer stopping the trajectory is enough to prevent the outcome.

question: A latent condition, as distinct from an active failure, is best described as:

options.text: A condition that only exists after an accident has already happened
The specific action or omission by the person at the controls at the moment of the occurrence
A failure that can only occur in automated systems
A weakness built into the system well before the event — a design flaw, a gap in training or an unworkable procedure — that lies dormant until it combines with something else

explanation: Latent conditions are seeded into the system long in advance by decisions made far from the sharp end — designers, managers, regulators — and may sit unnoticed for years. An active failure is the immediate, often human, act that triggers the outcome once the latent conditions are already in place.

question: An organization with a genuine "reporting culture" is one in which:

options.text: Every report automatically triggers disciplinary action
Reports are filed only after a regulator demands them
Staff are willing to report their own errors and safety concerns because they trust the information will be used to improve safety rather than to punish them
Only managers are permitted to file safety reports

explanation: A reporting culture depends on trust. If people believe that disclosing an error or a near-miss will be used against them, the reports simply stop coming, and the organization loses the early warning that reporting is meant to provide.

question: A "just culture" in a safety reporting system is one that:

options.text: Draws a clear line between honest mistakes, which are not punished, and reckless or deliberate violations, which are
Applies only to cabin crew, not to pilots
Treats every reported error identically to a deliberate violation
Never disciplines anyone under any circumstances, regardless of intent

explanation: A just culture is not a blame-free culture. It protects people who make honest errors or disclose them voluntarily, while still holding gross negligence or wilful violations to account — the distinction is what keeps reporting honest without becoming a shield for recklessness.

question: A "flexible culture", in the sense used when describing organizational safety culture, refers to an organization that:

options.text: Changes its safety policy every time a new manager is appointed
Allows staff to ignore standard operating procedures whenever they are inconvenient
Has no fixed procedures at all, leaving every decision to individual judgement
Can reconfigure itself from a normal hierarchy to a flatter, expert-led structure when a situation demands rapid, specialist decision-making

explanation: Flexibility here means the organization can shift authority toward whoever has the relevant expertise during an unusual or high-tempo event, then revert to its normal structure afterward — not that procedures are optional day to day.

question: A "learning culture" within a safety management system is one where the organization:

options.text: Only reviews safety data after a regulator issues a finding
Measures its success purely by the number of reports filed each year
Requires every employee to pass an annual written examination
Draws the right conclusions from its safety information and is willing to implement reform, rather than simply collecting reports

explanation: Collecting and reporting data is only useful if the organization actually acts on it. A learning culture closes the loop: it analyses what reports reveal and changes procedures, training or design in response.

question: In the Threat and Error Management (TEM) framework, a "threat" is defined as:

options.text: Any event or condition outside the influence of the flight crew that increases operational complexity and must be managed to maintain safety margins
Any action taken by the flight crew that deviates from a procedure
The final uncorrected state of the aircraft, such as being unstable on approach
A hypothetical scenario used only in simulator training, never in real operations

explanation: A threat originates outside the crew — weather, traffic, an aircraft malfunction, a rushed turnaround — and the crew's job is to detect and manage it before it produces a crew error or an undesired aircraft state.

question: Within TEM, how does an "error" differ from an "undesired aircraft state"?

options.text: An error can only be committed by air traffic control, never by the flight crew

An error is a crew action or inaction that leads away from the intended plan; an undesired aircraft state is the resulting position, speed, attitude or configuration that has reduced the margin of safety
An undesired aircraft state always happens before the error that causes it
They describe exactly the same thing at two different stages of a flight

explanation: The TEM chain runs threat → error → undesired aircraft state → outcome. The error is what the crew does (or fails to do); the undesired aircraft state is what that does to the aircraft's energy, position or configuration — for example, becoming unstable on approach after mishandling the threat of a late runway change.

question: The practical value of the TEM framework for a line crew is mainly that it:

options.text: Removes the need for standard operating procedures
Is used only by accident investigators after the fact, never by crews in real time
Replaces the need for a pre-flight briefing
Gives crews a structured way to anticipate threats and trap errors early, before they develop into an undesired aircraft state

explanation: TEM is a live, forward-looking tool: briefing expected threats, watching for the errors they tend to provoke, and catching an undesired aircraft state early — not a retrospective label applied only during an investigation.

question: Beyond the physical handling of the aircraft, which of the following is also a core duty of the flight crew from a human-factors standpoint?

options.text: Managing their own workload, monitoring each other, and maintaining situational awareness throughout the flight
Writing the aircraft's maintenance release
Personally refuelling the aircraft before every departure
Setting the airline's commercial pricing for the route being flown

explanation: Flying is only part of the task. Crews are also responsible for managing their own and each other's workload, cross-checking, and keeping a shared, accurate picture of the situation — duties that sit squarely inside human factors rather than stick-and-rudder skill.

question: Which piece of equipment is most often credited as the single most significant advance in flight safety of the modern era?

options.text: Cabin Wi-Fi
The Ground Proximity Warning System (and its terrain-awareness successors), which directly addresses controlled flight into terrain
In-flight entertainment systems
Weather radar colour displays

explanation: Controlled flight into terrain was, for decades, one of the largest categories of fatal accidents. Terrain-warning equipment gave crews a direct, timely alert against exactly that failure mode, and is widely credited with the sharpest single reduction in that accident category.

question: Human Factors, properly understood, applies to which of the following groups?

options.text: Flight crew, cabin crew, air traffic controllers, maintenance engineers and designers alike
Flight crew only
Only ground staff, since flight crew are separately covered by flight training
Only personnel who have been involved in a previous incident

explanation: Human Factors is relevant wherever a person interacts with the aviation system — in the cockpit, the cabin, the control tower, the hangar or the design office — not to one professional group alone.

question: Why does human performance training appear as a mandatory subject in professional pilot licensing syllabuses worldwide?

options.text: Because insurers, not regulators, require it
Because it is the easiest subject to examine
Because it replaced the need for a flight test
Because the proportion of accidents attributable to human performance made it a formally mandated part of licensing standards, rather than an optional extra

explanation: Once human performance was recognised as the leading contributor to accidents, its formal study became a required part of licensing standards for professional pilots, on the reasoning that a pilot who understands their own limitations is better placed to manage them.

question: A student notices that topics such as stress, fatigue and alcohol each affect several different areas of human performance (vision, decision making, reaction time). The best explanation is that:

options.text: Each topic is actually unrelated to the others and the overlap is an error
Only physical factors can affect more than one system; mental factors affect only one
The subject is organized this way purely by coincidence and has no real pattern
Human performance limitations are interconnected, so a single stressor can degrade several different systems at once rather than acting in isolation

explanation: The body and mind do not divide neatly along chapter lines. A stressor like fatigue can simultaneously blunt vision, narrow attention and slow decision making, which is exactly why the subject keeps returning to the same underlying factors from different angles.

question: Which statement about the Swiss Cheese model is correct?

options.text: The model was designed specifically to assign personal blame to the last person who touched the aircraft
The positions and sizes of the holes in each layer are dynamic, changing as procedures, staffing and equipment change over time
Once a defence is built, its weaknesses never change
The model assumes there is normally only one layer of defence between a threat and an accident

explanation: The holes are not static defects; they open and close as training lapses, procedures change, equipment ages or workload spikes. Multiple layers of defence exist precisely so that a gap in one layer, on its own, is not enough to let an accident trajectory through.

question: A crew briefs that the destination airport has a tailwind-favoured runway in use and a short taxi time, and agrees in advance how they will handle a possible late runway change. This is best described, in TEM terms, as:

options.text: Proactive threat management — anticipating a known threat and agreeing a plan before it can produce an error
An undesired aircraft state, because the runway is tailwind-favoured
Reactive error management, since the threat has not yet occurred
A violation, because it deviates from the published approach plate

explanation: Briefing a known, anticipated threat and agreeing a response ahead of time is the textbook case of managing a threat proactively — catching it before it has any chance to generate a crew error, rather than reacting after the fact.

question: An "undesired aircraft state" that is not recovered is most accurately described as:

options.text: A condition that, by definition, always ends in an accident
A deliberate test manoeuvre flown during training
A threat that originated from outside the aircraft
The last managed stage before an outcome such as an incident or accident

explanation: An undesired aircraft state is recoverable right up until it isn't. If it is neither detected nor corrected, it is the final link in the TEM chain before an outcome — but reaching that state does not by itself guarantee an accident; it only means the safety margin is already reduced.

question: The twin objectives most commonly used to summarize the purpose of Human Factors in aviation are:

options.text: Safety and efficiency of the operation, together with the well-being of the individual
Crew seniority and promotion criteria
Speed and fuel economy
Passenger comfort and on-time performance

explanation: Human Factors work is usually summarized as serving two linked goals: the safety and efficiency of the operation as a whole, and the health and well-being of the individual person doing the job.
